title: Paint Coverage Calculator: Liters per m² | Hacé Cuentas
h1: Calculate Paint Needed for Your Walls
description: Paint coverage calculator: find out exactly how many liters you need per m². Covers 1–2 coats, waste factor, and surface type tips.
intro:
Buying too little paint means an extra trip to the hardware store — and the risk of a color batch mismatch that ruins your finish. Buying too much wastes money and leaves you storing hazardous material. Getting the quantity right before you start is the single most underrated step in any painting project, yet most people still guess or over-rely on the salesperson at the paint counter.

Paint coverage — measured in square meters per liter — varies more than most homeowners realize. A bargain-bin interior latex might claim 12 m²/L on the label but deliver closer to 8 m²/L on a rough concrete wall. A premium exterior acrylic rated at 10 m²/L can stretch to 13 m²/L on a smooth, primed gypsum board. The difference between label coverage and real-world coverage comes down to four factors: surface porosity, surface texture, application method (roller, brush, or spray), and the paint's own solids content.

This calculator cuts through that complexity. Enter your total wall area in square meters and the coverage rate printed on your paint can (or use the 10–12 m²/L industry default if you haven't chosen a brand yet). The tool instantly tells you how many liters you need for one coat, and you can multiply for however many coats your project requires — typically two for finish paint and one for primer.

What makes this calculator genuinely useful beyond a simple division problem:

**Surface adjustments matter.** New drywall and raw masonry are highly porous and can absorb 30–50% more paint than a previously painted wall. If you're painting bare plaster or unprimed brick, mentally reduce the coverage rate by 20–30% and add a dedicated primer coat to your estimate.

**The 10% waste rule is real.** Even experienced painters lose material to roller splatter, tray residue, and touch-up patches. Always round your final liter count up and add a 10% buffer — that's roughly one extra liter for every 100–120 m² of wall area.

**Two coats is the professional standard.** A single coat rarely achieves opacity, especially when changing from a dark color to a light one or when covering water stains. Budget for two coats from the start rather than discovering mid-project that one coat isn't enough.

**Ceiling and trim paint differ.** Ceiling paints and semi-gloss trim paints often have different coverage rates than standard wall paint. If your project includes ceilings and baseboards, calculate them separately using the specific product's coverage data.

Whether you're a homeowner refreshing a bedroom, a contractor quoting a full apartment renovation, or a student learning construction estimating, this tool gives you a reliable starting point in under ten seconds — no registration, no ads blocking the result, and no data sent anywhere.
keyTakeaway: Formula: **Calculate paint needed per square meter of wall**. Direct application with your input values. Paint coverage: 1L covers 10-12 m² per coat. Typically 2 coats required.

useCases.title: Single-bedroom refresh with two coats
useCases.description: A 12 m² bedroom has four walls totaling approximately 42 m² of paintable surface (subtracting a standard door and window). Using a mid-range interior latex rated at 11 m²/L, the calculator returns 3.82 L per coat — round up to 4 L, then double for two coats: 8 L. One standard 10 L can covers the job with material left for touch-ups.

useCases.title: Open-plan living area with dark-to-light color change
useCases.description: A 35 m² open-plan space has roughly 110 m² of wall surface. Switching from charcoal gray to off-white requires a tinted primer coat plus two finish coats. Primer at 12 m²/L needs 9.2 L (one 10 L can). Finish paint at 10 m²/L needs 11 L per coat × 2 = 22 L. Total budget: one 10 L primer can + two 10 L finish cans + one 5 L finish can for safety margin.

useCases.title: Exterior facade on raw cement render
useCases.description: A two-story home exterior measures 280 m² including gable ends but excluding windows and doors (approximately 40 m² of openings). Raw cement is highly porous; use a reduced effective coverage of 8 m²/L for the first coat. First coat: 35 L. Second coat on sealed surface at 10 m²/L: 28 L. Total: 63 L — buy 65 L (six 10 L cans + one 5 L can) to stay safe.

useCases.title: Contractor quoting a 10-apartment building
useCases.description: Each apartment averages 180 m² of wall and ceiling surface. At 11 m²/L coverage and two coats, each unit needs 32.7 L — round to 34 L. Ten units = 340 L. Adding 10% waste buffer: 374 L. The contractor orders 38 × 10 L cans per color, negotiating a volume discount with the supplier using this documented estimate.

useCases.title: Garage floor epoxy coverage (adapted use case)
useCases.description: Epoxy floor coating is often rated at 5–6 m²/L because it's applied thicker than wall paint. A 50 m² garage floor at 5.5 m²/L needs 9.1 L for one coat and 18.2 L for two coats. Many epoxy systems come in 4 L kits, so the buyer needs five kits (20 L) to cover the floor twice with a small reserve.

useCases.title: School classroom renovation budget planning
useCases.description: A facilities manager overseeing 20 identical classrooms (each 58 m² wall area) uses the calculator to build a procurement request. At 10 m²/L and two coats: 11.6 L per room × 20 rooms = 232 L. Adding 10%: 255 L. The manager specifies this number in the tender document, preventing suppliers from over-quoting by 20–30% — a common practice when no estimate exists.

useCases.title: First-time DIYer learning to subtract openings
useCases.description: A new homeowner wants to paint a 4 m × 3 m room with 2.6 m ceilings. Total wall area = perimeter × height = 14 m × 2.6 m = 36.4 m². They subtract one door (2 m²) and two windows (1.5 m² each): 36.4 − 5 = 31.4 m². At 11 m²/L for two coats: 5.7 L. One 6 L can is sufficient. Without the subtraction step, they'd have bought a full 8 L and wasted 2.3 L.

useCases.title: Feature accent wall in a single bold color
useCases.description: An interior designer is painting one 12 m² feature wall in a deep navy — a saturated dark color that typically requires three coats over a white base to achieve full vibrancy. At 10 m²/L: 1.2 L per coat × 3 coats = 3.6 L. A single 4 L can is perfect. The designer notes for the client that the same calculation would apply for any highly pigmented or ombre technique requiring extra coats.

seoKeywords: how much paint do I need
explanation:
# Paint Coverage Calculator

Accurate material calculations for home improvement and construction projects prevent overspending and wasted trips to the hardware store. This calculator applies proven industry standards for paint coverage.

## How Paint Coverage Works

Paint coverage is typically measured in square meters per liter. Standard interior latex paint covers approximately 10-12 m² per liter with one coat. Professional results usually require two coats, so multiply your single-coat calculation by 2.

Factors that affect coverage include paint quality, wall texture, color intensity, and application technique. This calculator uses industry-standard estimates.

## How to Use This Calculator

1. Enter the total wall area you plan to paint (in m²)
2. Enter the coverage rate from your paint can (typically 10-12 m² per liter)
3. The calculator determines total liters needed for one coat
4. For professional results, plan for 2 coats

## Important Notes

This calculation is an estimate for reference purposes. For critical decisions, consult with a painting professional. Values are current as of 2026 and reviewed regularly.

faq.q: How do I calculate how many liters of paint I need for my walls?
faq.a: The core formula is: **Liters Needed = Wall Area (m²) ÷ Coverage Rate (m²/L)**. If your room has 60 m² of wall surface and your paint covers 10 m²/L, you need 6 L per coat. For two coats — the professional standard — you need 12 L. Always measure wall area carefully: multiply perimeter by ceiling height, then subtract the area of doors and windows. A standard interior door is about 1.8–2 m², and a typical window is 1.2–1.5 m². Skipping the subtraction step is the most common reason people over-buy paint.

faq.q: What is the standard paint coverage rate, and why does it vary so much?
faq.a: The industry standard for interior latex paint is 10–12 m² per liter, but real-world coverage depends on four key variables: (1) **Surface porosity** — raw concrete, new drywall, and bare plaster absorb far more paint than previously painted walls; (2) **Surface texture** — rough or heavily textured walls have greater actual surface area, consuming more paint; (3) **Application method** — sprayers deliver a thinner, more even coat than rollers, while brushes apply more material per stroke; (4) **Paint quality and solids content** — higher-quality paints have more pigment and binder solids, meaning they cover better per liter despite sometimes listing lower m²/L on the label. Always check the technical data sheet on the can rather than relying on the default.

faq.q: Do I always need two coats of paint?
faq.a: In most cases, yes. A single coat of standard latex rarely achieves full opacity or an even finish, particularly when: changing from a dark to a light color, covering water stains or smoke damage, painting over a glossy surface (without sanding or a bonding primer), or using a deeply saturated color that requires layering to build vibrancy. Where one coat may be sufficient: touch-ups on an identical color and finish, applying a third or fourth coat on a surface that already has good opacity, or using specialty high-build paints designed for single-coat application. Professional painters budget for two coats as the default and treat single-coat adequacy as a bonus, not a plan.

faq.q: What is the difference between primer and finish paint coverage?
faq.a: Primer and finish paint serve different purposes, and their coverage rates reflect that. Standard wall primers typically cover 10–14 m²/L because they're formulated to penetrate and seal the surface rather than build color depth — they're thinner and more fluid. Finish paints cover 8–12 m²/L and are formulated with pigment and binders for color accuracy and durability. The workflow for most projects is: one or two coats of primer (especially on new or porous surfaces) followed by two coats of finish paint. Calculate each product separately using its own coverage rate from the label. Skipping primer on raw surfaces often results in finish paint absorbing unevenly, creating a patchy look that requires extra coats to correct — costing more in the long run.

faq.q: How much extra paint should I buy as a buffer?
faq.a: The standard professional recommendation is a 10% waste allowance on top of your calculated need. This accounts for: roller splatter and tray residue (typically 3–5% of material), touch-up patches after the main job, uneven application in corners and edges, and small miscalculations in your area measurements. In practice, round your final liter count up to the nearest available can size and save any leftover paint in a well-sealed container for touch-ups. Label the can with the room name, color code, and brand — this is invaluable if you need to patch a wall a year later and can't remember the exact shade.

faq.q: How does surface texture affect how much paint I need?
faq.a: Texture dramatically affects consumption because a rough surface has significantly more real surface area than its flat measurement suggests. As a practical guide: **Smooth gypsum board or previously painted flat wall** — use the label coverage rate as stated. **Light texture (orange peel or fine stipple)** — reduce effective coverage by 10–15%. **Medium texture (knockdown or sand finish)** — reduce by 20–25%. **Heavy texture (rough plaster, old artex, or exterior brick)** — reduce by 30–40% and consider a fill primer or skim coat before painting. For spray application on textured surfaces, material consumption increases even further because overspray and surface irregularities waste more product. Adjust your estimate accordingly and err on the side of buying slightly more than the formula suggests.

faq.q: Should I subtract doors and windows from my wall area calculation?
faq.a: Yes — always subtract the area of openings for an accurate estimate. A standard interior door measures approximately 0.9 m × 2 m = 1.8 m², and a typical double interior door is about 3.6 m². A standard window is roughly 1.2 m × 1.0 m = 1.2 m². For a room with one door and two windows, you'd subtract approximately 4.2 m² from your total wall area. However, many painters deliberately skip this step and treat openings as a built-in safety buffer — the 'extra' paint covers door frames, window reveals, touch-ups, and waste. Both approaches are valid; what matters is being consistent so you don't both subtract openings *and* add a 10% buffer, which would result in a significant overestimate.

faq.q: How do I calculate paint for a ceiling separately from walls?
faq.a: Ceiling paint is a distinct product with its own coverage rate and is always calculated separately. To find your ceiling area, multiply length × width of the room (for a rectangular room). A 4 m × 5 m room has a 20 m² ceiling. Standard ceiling paint covers 10–12 m²/L, so one coat requires approximately 1.7–2 L and two coats require 3.4–4 L. Note that ceilings are typically painted with flat (matte) finish to hide imperfections and reduce glare, while walls use eggshell or satin. If your room has a vaulted or sloped ceiling, measure it as a series of rectangles or triangles and add the areas together rather than using a simple length × width formula.

faq.q: What's the difference in coverage between interior and exterior paints?
faq.a: Exterior paints generally have slightly lower coverage rates than interior paints — typically 8–10 m²/L versus 10–12 m²/L — for two main reasons. First, exterior surfaces (brick, cement render, wood siding, stucco) are usually rougher and more porous than interior walls. Second, exterior formulations are engineered with more flexible resins and UV stabilizers that add density to the paint, meaning there's more material per liter to lay down. When calculating exterior paint, always factor in the condition of the surface: a newly rendered wall in good condition might achieve 9 m²/L, while a weathered porous brick facade might only deliver 6–7 m²/L and require a dedicated masonry sealer as a first step. Check the manufacturer's technical sheet for the specific product and surface combination.

faq.q: Can I use this calculator for spray painting or airless sprayer applications?
faq.a: Yes, but with an important adjustment. Spray application — whether with a conventional air sprayer or an airless system — produces significantly more overspray and material loss than roller application. A standard roller application wastes approximately 5–10% of paint to splatter and residue. Airless sprayers lose 20–30% to overspray, especially near edges and in windy outdoor conditions. To adapt the calculator for spray application: take your calculated liter requirement and multiply by 1.25 (for a 25% overspray buffer). For example, if the calculator says you need 10 L by area, budget 12.5 L when spraying. Mask and sheet areas you don't intend to paint — overspray travels further than most people expect, and it's not always visible until it dries.

faq.q: How do I store leftover paint to preserve it for touch-ups?
faq.a: Proper storage can keep latex paint usable for 2–5 years. The key steps: (1) **Seal tightly** — place a piece of plastic wrap over the can opening before pressing the lid down, then tap the lid shut with a rubber mallet rather than a hammer to avoid deforming the rim. (2) **Store upside-down** for the first week — this creates an airtight seal with the paint itself inside the lid. (3) **Avoid temperature extremes** — store between 10°C and 25°C; latex paint is destroyed by freezing and degrades above 35°C. (4) **Label clearly** — write the room name, color name and code, brand, sheen level, and date of purchase on the can. When you use stored paint, stir well and test on a hidden area first — even properly stored paint can shift slightly in sheen or color over time.

faq.q: Why does the paint label coverage rate often differ from what I actually use?
faq.a: Paint labels are tested under ideal laboratory conditions: smooth, non-porous substrate, controlled temperature and humidity, and application by an experienced technician with calibrated equipment. Your conditions are almost certainly different. The most common reasons your real coverage falls short of the label: (1) Your walls are more porous or textured than the test substrate; (2) You apply paint thicker than the test (common with beginners using a heavily loaded roller); (3) Temperature and humidity affect how paint spreads and absorbs; (4) You're painting a highly saturated color that requires extra material to achieve opacity. As a rule of thumb, use 85–90% of the label coverage rate as your working estimate on a typical previously-painted interior wall, and 70–80% on raw or textured surfaces. This conservative approach means you'll rarely run short mid-project.
